modules.standard: Classify organisms using taxonomy: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Classify using the five-kingdom system, which sorts living things by cell type, body organisation and mode of nutrition. Monera: bacteria, prokaryotic. Protista: single-celled eukaryotes such as Amoeba. Fungi: absorb food, cell wall of chitin. Plantae: make food by photosynthesis. Animalia: eat food, no cell wall. Place a mushroom: Fungi.

Step 2, Learn the taxonomic hierarchy from largest to smallest group: Kingdom, Phylum (Division in plants), Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species. Each step down has fewer organisms that share more features. A handy memory line is built from the first letters K P C O F G S. Species is the basic unit: organisms that can breed together.

Step 3, Classify the lion: Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Chordata, Class Mammalia, Order Carnivora, Family Felidae, Genus Panthera, species leo. Check each rung: it has a backbone (Chordata), hair and milk glands (Mammalia), and meat-eating teeth (Carnivora). The domestic cat shares the same Class, Order and Family.

Step 4, Write the scientific name by binomial nomenclature: genus first with a capital letter, species second in lower case, and the whole name in italics or underlined when handwritten. Examples: Homo sapiens for human, Mangifera indica for mango, Panthera leo for lion. The two-part name is the same worldwide.

Step 5, Classify the mango tree: Kingdom Plantae, Division Angiospermae, Class Dicotyledonae, Order Sapindales, Family Anacardiaceae, Genus Mangifera, species indica. Explain why: it makes seeds inside fruits (angiosperm) and its seed has two cotyledons (dicot). Different plants in the genus share the name Mangifera.

Step 6, Your turn: the domestic cat is Felis catus. Name its genus, species, family and order, and say what it shares with the lion. Answer: genus Felis, species catus, family Felidae, order Carnivora. It shares Family Felidae, Order Carnivora, Class Mammalia, Phylum Chordata and Kingdom Animalia with the lion.

modules.standard: Compare major plant and animal groups: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Compare the five main plant groups. Algae: simple, mostly aquatic, for example Spirogyra. Bryophytes: moss and liverworts, no vascular tissue. Pteridophytes: ferns, vascular tissue but no seeds. Gymnosperms: Cycas and Pinus, seeds not enclosed in fruit. Angiosperms: flowering plants with seeds inside fruits.

Step 2, Compare bryophytes and pteridophytes. Both need water for the male gamete to swim to the egg. Moss has no true roots, only root-like rhizoids, and no xylem or phloem. A fern has true roots, stems, leaves and vascular tissue, so it can grow taller. Neither produces seeds; both spread by spores.

Step 3, Compare gymnosperms and angiosperms. Pine seeds sit naked on cone scales, while mango seeds are covered by a fruit. Angiosperms are divided into monocots (one seed leaf, parallel veins, fibrous roots, as in wheat) and dicots (two seed leaves, net veins, tap root, as in gram).

Step 4, Compare animal phyla by body plan. Porifera (sponges) have pores, no true tissues. Cnidaria (Hydra) have stinging cells and radial symmetry. Platyhelminthes (tapeworm) are flat. Annelida (earthworm) have ringed segments. Arthropoda (cockroach) have jointed legs and the most species. Mollusca (snail) have soft bodies. Echinodermata (starfish) have spiny skins.

Step 5, Compare the vertebrate classes by the heart. Pisces (fish) have gills and a 2-chambered heart. Amphibia (frog) have moist skin and a 3-chambered heart. Reptilia (lizard) have dry scales and usually a 3-chambered heart. Aves (sparrow) have feathers and a 4-chambered heart. Mammalia (human) have hair, milk glands and a 4-chambered heart.

Step 6, Your turn: compare a frog and a sparrow in four points: class, heart, skin or body covering, and body temperature. Answer: frog is Amphibia, 3-chambered heart, moist skin, cold-blooded; sparrow is Aves, 4-chambered heart, feathers, warm-blooded. Both are chordates with a backbone.

modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Structural organisation and cell: the unit of life', taught in a way that is with exam-style questions and written reasoning. The target is clear: describe tissues and cell structure. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.

modules.example: Solved: Plant cells have a cell wall and chloroplasts; animal cells do not. A tissue is a group of similar cells doing one job, for example muscle tissue for movement. Method: Model run for 'Structural organisation and cell: the unit of life'. Question: what do we want to find out? Prediction: one sentence. Method: three safe steps with the equipment named. Record: a small table with units. Conclusion: one sentence that uses the evidence and the key words of the unit. What a good answer looks like: a fair test, measured values with units, and a conclusion that matches the table.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Describe tissues and cell structure: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Describe the cell. All living things are made of cells, cells come from existing cells, and the cell is the basic unit. A prokaryotic cell (bacteria) has no membrane-bound nucleus. A eukaryotic cell (plant, animal) has a nucleus and organelles. Typical animal cells measure about 10 to 30 micrometres, and one micrometre is a thousandth of a millimetre.

Step 2, Describe the organelles. The cell membrane controls what enters and leaves. The nucleus holds DNA. Mitochondria release energy as ATP. Ribosomes make proteins. The endoplasmic reticulum transports materials, the Golgi body packs and sends them, and lysosomes digest waste. Write one job beside each name.

Step 3, Describe the differences between plant and animal cells. A plant cell has a cellulose cell wall outside the membrane, chloroplasts for photosynthesis and a large central vacuole. An animal cell has none of these but usually has centrioles, which help in cell division. Both have a nucleus, mitochondria and ribosomes.

Step 4, Describe the four animal tissues. Epithelial tissue covers surfaces, such as the flat cells lining the air sacs. Connective tissue joins and supports: bone, cartilage and blood. Muscular tissue contracts: skeletal, smooth and cardiac. Neural tissue carries signals through neurons. Plant tissues are meristematic (dividing) or permanent.

Step 5, Calculate magnification when you view a slide. Magnification = image size divided by actual size. A red blood cell about 7 micrometres wide is drawn 14 mm wide: 14 mm = 14,000 micrometres, and 14,000 / 7 = 2,000, so the drawing is magnified 2000 times. Safety: glass slides and coverslips are fragile, stains such as iodine stain skin and clothes, and hands are washed afterwards.

Step 6, Your turn: a cheek cell is 60 micrometres wide and your drawing is 30 mm wide. Find the magnification. Answer: 30 mm = 30,000 micrometres; 30,000 / 60 = 500, so the magnification is 500 times. Also say which organelle is absent from a cheek cell but present in a leaf cell: the chloroplast.

modules.standard: Explain mitosis, meiosis and biomolecules: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Follow the cell cycle: interphase (G1, S with DNA replication, G2) then M phase. In a 24 hour cycle, interphase takes about 23 hours and mitosis about 1 hour. A cell with 46 chromosomes copies its DNA in S phase.

Step 2, Describe mitosis: prophase (chromosomes condense), metaphase (align at the plate), anaphase (sister chromatids separate), telophase (nuclei form), and then cytokinesis. One 2n = 46 cell gives two cells with 46 chromosomes each.

Step 3, Describe meiosis. Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes with crossing over in prophase I, giving two cells with 23 chromosomes. Meiosis II separates chromatids, giving four haploid cells. Variation arises by crossing over and independent assortment.
Step 4, Count. Mitosis: 1 cell to 2 cells, DNA content 4C in G2 to 2C each. Meiosis: 1 cell to 4 cells, each with 1C. A human sperm cell has 23 chromosomes, and fertilisation restores 46.

Step 5, Cover biomolecules. Carbohydrates: glucose C6H12O6, starch, cellulose. Proteins: amino acids joined by peptide bonds. Lipids: glycerol and fatty acids. Nucleic acids: DNA with bases A, T, G, C. Enzymes lower activation energy.
Step 6, Your turn: a plant cell with 2n = 20 undergoes meiosis. How many chromosomes in each gamete cell and how many cells result? Answer: 10 chromosomes, 4 cells.

modules.standard: Describe photosynthesis, respiration and plant growth: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Describe photosynthesis with the balanced equation: 6CO2 + 6H2O gives C6H12O6 + 6O2, using light and chlorophyll. Count atoms to check: both sides have 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen and 18 oxygen. Carbon dioxide enters through stomata, water arrives through roots, glucose feeds the plant and oxygen is released.

Step 2, Describe the two stages. The light reaction happens in the grana of the chloroplast: light splits water, releasing oxygen and making ATP and NADPH. The dark reaction (Calvin cycle) happens in the stroma: carbon dioxide is fixed into sugar using that ATP and NADPH. Light is needed directly only for the first stage.

Step 3, Describe respiration: glucose + 6O2 gives 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy. Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm and splits one glucose into 2 pyruvate with a net gain of 2 ATP. The Krebs cycle runs in the mitochondrial matrix, and the electron transport chain on the inner membrane makes most of the ATP, about 36 to 38 in total.

Step 4, Describe plant growth and its regulators. Auxins promote cell elongation and make stems bend toward light. Gibberellins make stems elongate and break seed dormancy. Cytokinins promote cell division. Abscisic acid closes stomata in drought. Ethylene ripens fruit. Growth is measured by increase in height, mass or number of cells.

Step 5, Describe the starch test for photosynthesis. Take a leaf kept in light, boil it in water for a minute, then warm it in ethanol in a hot water bath to remove chlorophyll, and add iodine. Blue-black means starch is present. Safety: ethanol is flammable, so never heat it over a flame; use hot water, wear goggles, and keep iodine off the skin.

Step 6, Your turn: if a plant makes 3 molecules of glucose, how many molecules of carbon dioxide are used and oxygen released? Answer: 6 CO2 gives 1 glucose, so 3 glucose need 18 CO2 and release 18 O2 (6 x 3 for each). In respiration the same 18 O2 would be needed to break the sugar down.

modules.standard: Describe digestion, breathing, circulation and excretion: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Describe digestion. In the mouth, salivary amylase starts breaking starch into sugars. In the stomach, acid of about pH 1.5 to 2 and the enzyme pepsin begin digesting protein. In the small intestine, bile, lipase and trypsin finish fats and proteins, and villi absorb the nutrients into the blood. Undigested matter leaves via the large intestine.

Step 2, Describe breathing. The diaphragm contracts and flattens, the ribs move up and out, chest volume rises, pressure falls and air flows in. In the alveoli oxygen diffuses into blood and carbon dioxide leaves. A resting adult takes in about 500 mL per breath (tidal volume) at roughly 12 breaths per minute: 500 x 12 = 6,000 mL, or 6 litres per minute.

Step 3, Describe circulation. The heart has four chambers. Deoxygenated blood enters the right atrium, goes to the right ventricle, then to the lungs. Oxygenated blood returns to the left atrium, enters the left ventricle and is pumped to the body. This double circulation keeps oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood apart.

Step 4, Describe the output of the heart. If each beat pumps about 70 mL (stroke volume) and the pulse is 72 beats per minute, then 70 x 72 = 5,040 mL, about 5 litres per minute. That is roughly the volume of blood in the whole body, so all of it passes the heart about once every minute.

Step 5, Describe excretion. Each kidney has about a million nephrons. Blood is filtered in the glomerulus to give roughly 180 litres of filtrate a day, but most water and useful solutes such as glucose are reabsorbed, so only about 1.5 litres of urine is made. Urea and extra salts leave, and urine passes through the ureters to the bladder.

Step 6, Your turn: a person breathes 450 mL per breath at 14 breaths a minute. Find the volume of air per minute, then name the muscle that pulls air in. Answer: 450 x 14 = 6,300 mL, which is 6.3 litres per minute. The muscle is the diaphragm, helped by the muscles between the ribs.
